title: Declaration Files (.d.ts)
summary: **Declaration files** (`.d.ts`) describe the *types* of JavaScript without any implementation, using the `declare` keyword. They let TypeScript understand untyped libraries — via `@types`/DefinitelyTyped, ambient declarations, and module augmentation.

subtopics.title: What .d.ts files are
subtopics.explanation: A .d.ts file contains only type information — no runtime code is emitted from it. It describes the shape of values that exist elsewhere (a JS library, a global, your own compiled output). The compiler emits .d.ts for your own library so consumers get types; you also write them by hand to type code that has none.
subtopics.example:
// math.d.ts
export declare function add(a: number, b: number): number;

subtopics.title: The declare keyword
subtopics.explanation: declare introduces an ambient declaration: it tells the compiler 'this thing exists at runtime, trust me' without generating code. Use it for globals (declare const VERSION: string), module shapes, or to describe APIs provided by the environment. It is the core building block of every declaration file.
subtopics.example:
declare const __APP_VERSION__: string;
declare function gtag(...args: unknown[]): void;

subtopics.title: Typing JS libraries with @types / DefinitelyTyped
subtopics.explanation: DefinitelyTyped is a community repo of .d.ts files for thousands of untyped packages, published under the @types scope (e.g. npm i -D @types/lodash). TypeScript auto-discovers @types packages, so installing one is usually all you need to get full typings for an otherwise untyped library.
subtopics.example:
// terminal: npm i -D @types/lodash
import _ from 'lodash'; // now fully typed

subtopics.title: Ambient declarations
subtopics.explanation: Ambient declarations describe things that exist globally or come from non-code imports. declare global { interface Window { myFlag: boolean } } adds to the global scope; declare module '*.svg' types asset imports. They live in .d.ts files included by the project and require no import to take effect.

subtopics.title: Module augmentation
subtopics.explanation: Module augmentation extends an existing module's types from your own code: open the module with declare module 'name' and add new members (e.g. a plugin adds a method to express's Request, or a field to a library interface). It merges with the original declarations instead of replacing them.

subtopics.title: Writing types for an untyped module
subtopics.explanation: When a package has no types and no @types entry, you write a small .d.ts: declare module 'pkg-name' and export the functions/values you use with your best-guess types. Start narrow (just what you call), tighten over time, and prefer unknown over any so unsafe usage is still flagged.

foundations.overview: Declaration files are how TypeScript knows about code it cannot see the types of: untyped JavaScript libraries, global variables injected by the environment, non-code imports, and your own published packages. They contain only type information via the declare keyword and are erased at runtime. Together with DefinitelyTyped's @types packages and module augmentation, they let a strict TypeScript project interoperate with the entire JavaScript ecosystem.
foundations.formalDefinition: A declaration file (.d.ts) is a TypeScript file that contains only ambient (non-emitting) declarations describing the types of values, functions, classes, modules, and globals that exist at runtime. The declare keyword marks a declaration as ambient, asserting existence without providing an implementation.
foundations.whyItMatters: Real apps depend on JavaScript libraries, browser/runtime globals, and bundler features that ship no types. Declaration files — written by hand, generated, or installed via @types — are what make these usable safely in strict TypeScript, and authoring them is a hallmark of advanced TS competence and a common senior interview topic.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a .d.ts as a contract or 'type-only header file' (like C's .h): it promises what exists at runtime so the compiler can check your usage, while the actual code lives elsewhere. declare means 'this already exists — just record its type.'
foundations.browserPerspective: Declaration files never reach the browser; they emit nothing. They are how you type browser-provided globals (window, document via lib 'DOM') and runtime-injected values (analytics globals, build-time constants), all of which exist at runtime but have no TypeScript source.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Installing @types/* for untyped npm packages, declaring module '*.svg'/'*.css' for asset imports, augmenting express's Request with a user field, typing a build-time global like __APP_VERSION__, and shipping generated .d.ts so consumers of your library get types.
foundations.businessImpact: Good declarations let teams adopt any library safely, preventing integration bugs and the cost of debugging untyped third-party code in production. Published types make your own packages adoptable and reduce consumer support burden.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Declaration files keep strict mode intact even at the boundary with untyped code, instead of forcing any everywhere. Module augmentation lets teams extend library types cleanly rather than casting.
foundations.performanceImpact: Zero runtime impact — .d.ts files emit no code. They affect type-check time: very large or deeply recursive declaration sets slow tsc, which skipLibCheck can mitigate for third-party .d.ts.
commonUseCases: Installing @types/* to type an untyped npm package
Declaring asset imports (*.svg, *.css) and build-time globals
Augmenting a library's types (e.g. express Request.user)
Shipping generated .d.ts so consumers of your library get types

commonMisconceptions.reality: It contains only ambient type declarations and emits nothing; the actual implementation lives in real JS/TS elsewhere.

commonMisconceptions.myth: declare creates the value at runtime.
commonMisconceptions.reality: declare only asserts that a value already exists; if it doesn't, you get a runtime error despite passing type-checking.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Module augmentation replaces the library's types.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Augmentation merges with the original declarations (declaration merging); you add to them, you don't overwrite them.

config.intro: Follow import _ from 'lodash' through type discovery and checking.

steps.name: Resolve the module
steps.detail: TypeScript resolves 'lodash' to node_modules/lodash and looks for bundled types (a types field / index.d.ts).

steps.name: Look for @types
steps.detail: If none are bundled, it checks node_modules/@types/lodash from DefinitelyTyped.

steps.name: Check local declarations
steps.detail: It also considers your own .d.ts ambient module declarations for the package name.

steps.name: Apply the declarations
steps.detail: The found .d.ts describes the exported functions/types; the compiler uses them to type your import.

steps.name: Type-check usage
steps.detail: Calls like _.chunk([1,2,3], 2) are checked against the declared signatures.

steps.name: Erase at emit
steps.detail: All declarations are type-only and emit nothing — the runtime just imports the real lodash.

interactiveExamples.title: Module augmentation (declaration merging)

codeLab.title: Write a declaration for an untyped module
codeLab.instructions: Sketch a .d.ts for an untyped 'slugify' package exposing one function slug(s: string): string, then use it. (The sandbox runs the JS implementation it would describe.)
hints: Open the module with declare module 'slugify' { ... }.
Inside, export the function signatures you call, e.g. export function slug(input: string): string;

debuggingLab.title: Augmentation that overwrites instead of merging
debuggingLab.symptom: A wrong declare module replaces a library's types so its real exports become unknown, breaking valid calls.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Writing a fresh declare module for a package that already has types (or declaring only some exports) makes the compiler treat that as the module's complete type, hiding the rest. format() then appears to not exist. The fix is to augment additively or declare every export you rely on.
commonMistakes: Re-declaring a typed module and accidentally dropping its real exports.
Confusing augmentation (additive, merges) with a full standalone declaration.
Declaring only some exports and assuming the rest still come through.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Augment the module additively (or declare all used exports) so both parse and format remain typed.

theory.question: What is a .d.ts file and what is the role of the declare keyword?
theory.directAnswer: A .d.ts is a declaration file containing only type information — no implementation — so it emits no runtime code. It describes the types of values that exist elsewhere: JS libraries, globals, your compiled output. declare marks a declaration as ambient, asserting that the value exists at runtime without generating code for it. Together they let TypeScript type-check against code it can't see the source of.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A type-only file of ambient declarations describing runtime shapes.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: So strict TypeScript can interoperate safely with untyped JS, globals, and the wider ecosystem.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler reads .d.ts files (yours, bundled, or @types), applies the declared types to matching imports/globals, checks usage, and emits nothing from them.

theory.whyImportant: Every nontrivial app consumes untyped JS or environment globals; declaration files are the safe bridge instead of any.
theory.realWorldExample: Generated .d.ts shipped with an npm package give its consumers full IntelliSense without the source.

nestedTopics.title: Generated vs hand-written
nestedTopics.explanation: declaration:true emits .d.ts from your code; you hand-write them for untyped third-party code.

nestedTopics.title: Ambient vs module
nestedTopics.explanation: Global ambient declarations need no import; module declarations apply to a specific import specifier.

followUps.question: Does declare create the value?
followUps.answer: No — it only asserts the value exists; if it doesn't actually exist at runtime, you'll get a runtime error despite passing type-checking.

theory.question: What are DefinitelyTyped and @types, and how does TypeScript pick up types for an untyped package?
theory.directAnswer: DefinitelyTyped is a community-maintained repository of declaration files for packages that don't ship their own, published to npm under the @types scope (e.g. @types/lodash). When you import a package, TypeScript first looks for types bundled with it, then for a matching @types package in node_modules, then for your own ambient declarations — using whichever it finds to type the import.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A central source of community .d.ts published as @types/* packages, auto-discovered by the compiler.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Most older or small JS packages ship no types; @types provides them without changing the original package.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: typeRoots defaults to node_modules/@types; the resolver checks bundled types, then @types, then local declarations for the module name.

theory.whyImportant: Knowing the lookup order explains why installing one @types package fixes typing — and why a stale @types version causes mismatches.
theory.realWorldExample: npm i -D @types/node gives full typings for Node's built-in modules in a backend or tooling project.

nestedTopics.title: types vs typeRoots
nestedTopics.explanation: types restricts which @types packages are included; typeRoots changes where they're found.

nestedTopics.title: Version skew
nestedTopics.explanation: @types versions can lag the library, causing signature mismatches.

followUps.question: What if no @types exists?
followUps.answer: Write your own minimal declare module '...' .d.ts for the parts you use, or contribute types upstream/to DefinitelyTyped.

scenario.question: A small npm package you must use ships no types and has no @types entry, but the team's strict config forbids any. How do you integrate it safely?
scenario.directAnswer: Write a local declaration file: create types/tiny-lib.d.ts with declare module 'tiny-lib' and declare just the exports you actually call, using precise types (prefer unknown over any for fuzzy parts). Include the file via tsconfig (typeRoots/include) so the ambient module is picked up. Tighten the signatures over time and consider contributing them to DefinitelyTyped.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A hand-written ambient module declaration for an untyped dependency.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Strict mode bans implicit any, so the untyped import must be given explicit types.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: declare module 'name' creates an ambient module the resolver matches to that specifier, supplying types without touching the package.

scenario.whyImportant: This is the standard senior-level technique for keeping strictness while using the long tail of untyped npm.

nestedTopics.title: Narrow first
nestedTopics.explanation: Declare only what you use; expand as needed.

nestedTopics.title: unknown over any
nestedTopics.explanation: Forces callers to narrow, preserving safety where you're unsure of the shape.

followUps.question: Where should the .d.ts live?
followUps.answer: In a project folder included by tsconfig (e.g. src/types or a typeRoots entry) so the compiler loads the ambient declaration.

coding.question: Write the ambient declarations to (a) type SVG imports as a string default export and (b) augment the global Window with an analytics function. Then show usage.
coding.thoughtProcess: Asset imports need a wildcard ambient module (declare module '*.svg') exporting a default string. Adding to globals needs declare global with an interface Window member, which merges via declaration merging. Both are type-only; the runtime just uses the real values the bundler/host provides.
coding.lineByLine: declare module '*.svg' wildcard-matches any .svg import and types its default as a string. declare global with interface Window merges a track method into the global Window type. export {} turns the file into a module so declare global is permitted. At runtime the bundler supplies the URL and the host supplies window.track.

alternativeApproaches.title: Per-asset typing
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Instead of a wildcard, declare specific modules, but the wildcard scales better for many assets.
alternativeApproaches.code: // declare module './logo.svg' { const s: string; export default s; }

followUps.question: Why is export {} needed for declare global?
followUps.answer: declare global is only allowed inside a module; an otherwise script-scoped .d.ts needs a top-level import/export (export {}) to count as a module.

systemDesign.question: Design the type-distribution strategy for a shared TypeScript SDK/library consumed by many internal apps, some on bundlers and some on native Node ESM. How do you ship and maintain its declaration files?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Author the library in TypeScript with declaration: true (and declarationMap for go-to-definition), emitting .d.ts alongside the JS and pointing package.json's types/typesVersions and exports map at them. Provide both ESM and CJS outputs with matching .d.ts/.d.mts so every consumer environment resolves types correctly. Keep public types narrow and stable, version them with the package (semver), gate changes behind API-extractor or tsc --noEmit in CI to catch breaking type changes, and document module augmentation points for consumers who extend the SDK.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An architecture for generating, packaging, and versioning a library's declaration files across consumer runtimes.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Consumers differ (bundler vs nodenext, ESM vs CJS); types must resolve in all of them and stay stable across releases.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Generated .d.ts (and .d.mts/.d.cts) are referenced via the package.json exports/types map; CI tools detect public API drift; semver communicates breaking type changes.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Type stability of a shared SDK affects every downstream team; a careless declaration change silently breaks many builds at once.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A design-system or API-client package ships dual ESM/CJS builds with matching declarations and an exports map so React apps and Node services both get correct types.

nestedTopics.title: exports map
nestedTopics.explanation: package.json exports routes each consumer (import/require) to the right JS and matching .d.ts.

nestedTopics.title: API extraction
nestedTopics.explanation: Tools like API Extractor freeze and diff the public type surface to catch accidental breaks.

nestedTopics.title: Augmentation contract
nestedTopics.explanation: Document which interfaces consumers may augment so extension points stay stable.

followUps.question: How do you prevent accidental breaking type changes?
followUps.answer: Run a public-API snapshot/diff (e.g. API Extractor) plus downstream tsc --noEmit in CI, and treat type-surface changes as semver-significant.

followUps.question: Why ship both .d.ts and .d.mts?
followUps.answer: Node's ESM/CJS resolution picks declarations by extension/conditions; matching them to each output ensures types resolve under both nodenext and bundler resolution.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Declaration files form the typed boundary between your code and everything it can't see: third-party JS, environment globals, and your own published packages. A typical layout has a src/types/ folder for project-wide ambient declarations (assets, globals, augmentations) plus generated .d.ts for any library you publish.
productionDeepDive.performance: No runtime cost — .d.ts emit nothing. They contribute to type-check time; very large third-party declaration sets can slow tsc, mitigated with skipLibCheck (skips checking .d.ts) while still using them for typing.
productionDeepDive.security: Declarations describe shapes but don't validate runtime data; trusting a declared type for untrusted input (e.g. a parsed response from an untyped lib) can hide malformed data — pair with runtime validation. Incorrect declarations can also mask real type mismatches.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Centralize shared ambient declarations and augmentations so they aren't duplicated; for published libraries, automate .d.ts generation and diff the public API surface to prevent accidental breaking changes across many consumers.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Keep hand-written declarations minimal and precise (declare only what you use, prefer unknown over any), and prefer @types or upstream-shipped types over local declarations when available so they stay current.
productionDeepDive.observability: tsc --noEmit catches declaration mismatches; declarationMap enables go-to-definition into source; API-surface diff tools surface unintended public type changes in CI.

caseStudies.problem: Thousands of popular JS libraries shipped no types, blocking safe adoption in TypeScript.
caseStudies.solution: A community repo of .d.ts published as @types/* packages, auto-discovered by the compiler.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Types can lag the library version (skew), but the coverage unlocked the entire npm ecosystem for TS.
caseStudies.lessons: Separating types from implementation lets the community type code it doesn't own, and version skew must be managed deliberately.

keyTakeaways: A .d.ts file holds only ambient type declarations and emits no runtime code; declare asserts a value exists without creating it.
DefinitelyTyped publishes community types as @types/* packages that TypeScript auto-discovers for untyped libraries.
Ambient declarations type globals and non-code imports (*.svg, *.css); they need no import to take effect.
Module augmentation merges with a library's existing types (declaration merging) rather than replacing them.
For an untyped package with no @types, write a minimal declare module — declare what you use, prefer unknown over any.
